column2: The sixth prefatory discussion: on the kinds of human perceivers, by innate disposition or by spiritual exercise, with a preliminary discussion of revelation and dream vision

Know that God, glory be to Him, chose from among human beings certain individuals whom He favored with His address and created with an innate disposition to know Him, and He made them intermediaries between Himself and His servants. They make known to them what serves their interests, urge them toward their guidance, take hold of their waistbands to hold them back from the Fire, and show them the way of salvation. Among the knowledge that He casts to them, and among the extraordinary acts that He brings out on their tongues, were reports of events hidden from human beings, which cannot be known except from God through their mediation, and which they themselves know only because God taught them. The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said: “Indeed, I know only what God has taught me.” Know that their reporting in this matter has truthfulness as its property and its necessity, as will become clear to you when we explain the reality of prophecy. A sign of this kind of human being is that, in the state of revelation, there is found in them an absence from those present with them, with a snoring sound, as if it were a swoon or a faint to the eye, though it is nothing of the kind. In truth it is an absorption in meeting the spiritual angel, by means of a perception suited to them that lies wholly outside the human faculties of perception. Then he descends to the human faculties of perception, either by hearing a humming of speech, which he comes to understand, or by the form of a person appearing to him and addressing him with what he has brought from God. Then that state clears away from him, and he has already

retained what was cast to him. The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said, when he was asked about revelation: “Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and that is the hardest on me; then it leaves me, and I have retained what was said. And sometimes the angel appears to me as a man and speaks to me, and I retain what he says.” During this he is overtaken by a hardship and a squeezing that cannot be put into words. In the hadith: “He used to undergo hardship from the sending down.” ʿĀʾisha said: “Revelation would come down on him on a very cold day, and then leave him, and his forehead would be streaming with sweat.” And the Exalted said: “We shall cast upon you a weighty word” (73: 5). Because of this extremity in the coming down of revelation, the polytheists used to accuse the prophets of madness and say of him, “He has a familiar spirit or a follower from the jinn.” They were only confused by what they saw of the outward aspect of those states; and whoever God leads astray has no guide.

Another of their signs is that before revelation there are found in them goodness of character and purity and a keeping away from everything blameworthy and all that is unclean. This is the meaning of infallibility (ʿiṣma). It is as though he were innately disposed to keep clear of blameworthy things and to be repelled by them, as though they were contrary to his constitution. It is in the Ṣaḥīḥ that as a boy he carried stones with his uncle al-ʿAbbās for the building of the Kaʿba, and put them in his lower garment; he was uncovered and fell down in a faint, until he covered himself with his garment. And he was invited to a gathering at a feast where there was a wedding and amusement, and a drowsiness of sleep came over him until the sun rose, and he was present at nothing of their doings. Rather, God kept him clear of all that, so that by his constitution he even kept clear of foods that are disliked: the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, would not go near onions or garlic. He was asked about that and said, “I speak in confidence with one with whom you do not.” And consider that when the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, told Khadīja, may God be pleased with her, about the state of revelation when it first came upon him suddenly, she wished to test him and said, “Place me between you and your garment.” When he did that, it went away from him. She said, “It is an angel and not a devil,” meaning that the angel does not approach women. Likewise she asked him in what clothing he most liked it to come to him, and he said, “White and green.” She said, “It is the angel,” meaning that white and green are among the colors of good and of angels, and black among the colors of evil and of devils, and the like.

Another of their signs is their calling to religion and worship, namely prayer, charity and chastity. Khadīja inferred from that the truthfulness of the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, and so did Abū Bakr; neither of them needed, in his case, any proof outside his state and his character. And it is in the Ṣaḥīḥ that when the letter of the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, came to Heraclius, calling him to Islam, he summoned those of Quraysh who were found in his country, among them Abū Sufyān, to ask them about his condition. Among what he asked was: “What does he command you?” Abū Sufyān said: “Prayer, almsgiving, the keeping of kinship ties, and chastity,” and so on to the end of what he asked, and he answered him. Then [Heraclius] said: “If what you say is true, he is a prophet, and he will rule what is under these two feet of mine.” The chastity to which Heraclius alluded is infallibility. See how he took from infallibility and from the call to religion and worship a proof of the soundness of his prophethood and did not need a miracle, which shows that this is among the signs of prophecy.

Another of their signs is that they are of noble lineage among their people. In the Ṣaḥīḥ: “God sent no prophet except within the protective strength of his people,” and in another version, “within the abundance of his people” — al-Ḥākim recorded it as a supplement to the two Ṣaḥīḥs. And in Heraclius’s question to Abū Sufyān, as it stands in the Ṣaḥīḥ, he said, “What is he like among you?” Abū Sufyān said, “He is of noble lineage among us.” Heraclius said, “Messengers are sent among the noble lineages of their peoples.” The meaning is that he has group solidarity (ʿaṣabiyya) and might that protect him from the harm of the unbelievers until he conveys the message of his Lord and God’s purpose is accomplished in the perfecting of His religion and His creed. Another of their signs is the occurrence of extraordinary acts for them, bearing witness to their truthfulness. These are acts that human beings are unable to produce the like of, and that is why they are called a miracle (muʿjiza, “incapacitating”). They are not of the kind within the power of servants; they occur only outside the sphere of their power. People differ over how they occur and how they indicate the confirmation of the prophets. The theologians, on the basis of the doctrine of the free agent, hold that they occur by God’s power and not by the act of the prophet; and although, according to the Muʿtazila, the acts of servants proceed from the servants, the miracle is not of the kind of their acts. According to the rest of the theologians, the prophet has no part in it except the challenge (taḥaddī) made with it by God’s permission, which is that the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, uses it as evidence, before

its occurrence, of his truthfulness in what he claims. When it occurs, it takes the place of an explicit statement from God that he is truthful, and its indication of truthfulness is then decisive. The miracle, then, is that which indicates by the combination of the extraordinary act and the challenge. For that reason the challenge is a part of it, and in the theologians’ expression it is the essential attribute of the miracle itself; this is a single thing, since that is the meaning of “essential” for them. The challenge is what distinguishes the miracle from the saintly wonder (karāma) and from sorcery, since neither of these needs confirmation, so there is no challenge in them unless it happens by chance. And if a challenge occurs in a saintly wonder, according to those who allow it, and it has an indication, that indication is only of sainthood, which is not prophecy. For this reason the Master Abū Isḥāq and others denied that extraordinary acts occur as saintly wonders, to avoid confusion with prophecy when a challenge is made on the basis of sainthood. We have shown you the difference between them, and that he [the saint] makes his challenge with something other than that with which the prophet makes his challenge, so there is no confusion. Besides, the report from the Master on this is not explicit, and it may be taken as a denial that the extraordinary acts of the prophets occur for them [the saints], on the ground that each of the two groups has its own extraordinary acts.

As for the Muʿtazila, what prevents the occurrence of saintly wonders in their view is that extraordinary acts are not among the acts of servants, and the servants’ acts are habitual, so there is no difference. As for their occurring at the hand of a liar for the purpose of deception, that is impossible. According to the Ashʿarites, this is because the essential attribute of the miracle itself is confirmation and guidance; were it to occur otherwise, the proof would become a specious doubt, guidance error and confirmation falsehood, realities would be transmuted and essential attributes reversed, and whatever entails an impossibility if its occurrence is supposed cannot be possible. According to the Muʿtazila, it is because the proof’s becoming a specious doubt and guidance’s becoming error is reprehensible, and so it does not occur from God. As for the philosophers, the extraordinary act in their view is the act of the prophet, even though it lies outside the sphere of power, on the basis of their doctrine of essential necessitation; and the occurrence of events, one from another, depends on originated causes and conditions that in the end rest on the Necessary Being, who acts by essence and not by choice. The prophetic soul, in their view, has essential properties, among them the issuing of these extraordinary acts by his power and the obedience of the elements to him in generation; and the prophet, in their view, is innately constituted to exercise control over generated things whenever he turns to them and gathers himself for them, through what God has made for him of that. The extraordinary act, in their view, occurs for the prophet whether or not it is for a challenge

and it bears witness to his truthfulness in that it indicates the prophet’s control over generated things, which is one of the properties of the prophetic soul, not in that it takes the place of an explicit statement of confirmation. For that reason its indication is not decisive in their view, as it is in the view of the theologians, the challenge is not a part of the miracle, and the challenge does not hold good as what distinguishes it from sorcery and from the saintly wonder. What distinguishes it from sorcery, in their view, is that the prophet is innately constituted for acts of good and turned away from acts of evil, so evil does not touch his extraordinary acts, whereas the sorcerer is the opposite: all his acts are evil and aimed at evil ends. What distinguishes it from the saintly wonder is that the extraordinary acts of the prophet are special, such as ascending to heaven, passing through dense bodies, raising the dead, speaking with angels and flying through the air, while the extraordinary acts of the saint are less than that, such as multiplying a small amount, speaking about some of the future, and the like, which fall short of the prophets’ control. The prophet can bring about all the extraordinary acts of the saint, while the saint is not able to do the like of the extraordinary acts of the prophets. The Sufis have established this in what they have written about their way and learned from those who informed them. Once this is established, know that the greatest of miracles, the noblest and the clearest in indication, is the noble Qurʾān sent down to our Prophet Muḥammad, God bless him and grant him peace. For extraordinary acts generally occur apart from the revelation that the prophet receives, and he brings the miracle as a witness to his truthfulness; the Qurʾān, however, is itself the revelation that is claimed and is itself the extraordinary, incapacitating act, so its witness is in its very self

and it does not need a proof distinct from it, as the other miracles do together with revelation, so its indication is the clearest, since the proof and the thing proved are united in it. This is the meaning of his saying, God bless him and grant him peace: “There is no prophet among the prophets who was not given signs the like of which human beings believed on account of; and what I was given was only a revelation that God revealed to me, so I hope to be the one among them with the most followers on the Day of Resurrection.” He is pointing out that when the miracle is of this degree of clarity and strength of indication, in being the revelation itself, the acceptance of its truth was the greater by reason of its clarity, and so those who accept it as true and believe, that is the followers and the community, were many.

Let us now give the explanation of the reality of prophecy as many of the verifying scholars have set it out, then the reality of soothsaying, then dream vision, then the matter of the diviners and other faculties of perception of the unseen, and so we say

Know — may God guide us and you — that we observe this world, with all the creatures in it, to be in a state of order and firm construction, with causes linked to their effects, generated things connected with generated things, and some existing things transformed into others; its wonders in this never end and its limits are never reached. I begin, of this, with the perceptible bodily world, and first the world of the observable elements, how it proceeds by degrees, ascending from earth to water, then to air, then to fire, each joined to the next, and each of them disposed to be transformed into what adjoins it, upward and downward, and at times it is transformed; and the higher of them is subtler than what precedes it, until it reaches the world of the celestial spheres, which is subtler than all, in layers joined one to another, in a configuration of which the senses perceive only the motions. By these some are guided to knowledge of the spheres’ magnitudes and positions, and, beyond that, of the existence of the essences that have these effects in them. Then look at the world of generation, how it begins with the minerals, then plants, then animals, in a wondrous gradation: the last horizon of the minerals is joined to the first horizon of the plants, such as grasses and what has no seed, and the last horizon of the plants, such as the palm and the vine, is joined to the first horizon of the animals, such as the snail and the shellfish, in which only the faculty of touch is found;

and the meaning of the connection among these generated things is that the last horizon of each is prepared, by a remarkable aptitude, to become the first horizon of the one after it. The animal world became vast and its kinds many, and it ended, in the gradation of generation, at man, the possessor of thought and reflection, rising to him from the world of power (qudra), in which sensation and perception are combined but which has not reached reflection and thought in actuality; and that was the first horizon of man, after it. And this is the limit of our observation. Then we find in the worlds, for all their differences, various effects: in the world of sense, effects of the motions of the spheres and the elements, and in the world of generation, effects of the motion of growth and of perception, all of which bear witness that they have an agent distinct from bodies, which is therefore spiritual, and which is joined to generated things because this world is continuous in their existence; and for that reason it is the perceiving and moving soul. Above it there must be another existence that gives it the powers of perception and motion and is also joined to it, whose essence is pure perception and sheer intellection; and this is the world of the angels. It follows from this that the soul has an aptitude for stripping itself of humanity (insilākh) into angelhood, so as to become in actuality, at some time, in a flash, of the kind of the angels, and that after its spiritual essence is perfected in actuality, as we shall mention later; and that it has a connection with the horizon after it, as is the way of ordered existing things, as we explained earlier. So it has in this connection two directions, upward and downward

and it is joined to the body from below it, and through it acquires the sensory faculties of perception by which it is made ready to attain intellection in actuality; and from the side above it, it is joined to the horizon of the angels and through it acquires the perceptions of knowledge and of the unseen, for the world of events exists in their intellections without time. This accords with what we presented earlier of the firm order in existence, through the connection of its essences and powers with one another. Then this human soul is hidden from sight, while its effects are apparent in the body, so that it is as though the body and all its parts, together and apart, were instruments of the soul and its powers. As for the active ones: grasping with the hand, walking with the foot, speaking with the tongue, and the movement of the whole by the body, one part pushing another along. As for the perceptive ones, although the powers of perception are arranged and ascend to the highest power among them, that of the faculty of thought, which is called rationality, the powers of the outer sense, with its instruments of hearing, sight and the rest, ascend to the inner, the first of which is the common sense, a power that perceives sensed things, seen, heard, touched and the rest, in a single state; and in that respect it differs from the power of outer sense, because sensed things do not crowd upon it at one time. Then the common sense passes it on to imagination, which is a power that represents the sensed thing in the soul as it is, abstracted only from external matter. The instrument of these two powers in their operation is the first ventricle of the brain, its front part for the first

and its rear part for the second. Then imagination ascends to estimation and memory. Estimation is for perceiving the meanings related to individuals, such as the enmity of Zayd, the friendship of ʿAmr, the compassion of a father, and the predation of a wolf; and memory is for storing all perceptions as imagined, and for them it is like a storehouse, keeping them until the time they are needed. The instrument of these two powers in their operation is the rear ventricle of the brain, its front part for the first and its rear part for the other. Then all of them ascend to the power of thought, whose instrument is the middle ventricle of the brain; it is the power through which the movement of reflection and the turning toward intellection occur, and through it the soul is constantly set in motion by the longing implanted in it to be freed from the lowly state of potentiality and aptitude that belongs to humanity. It passes into actuality in its intellection, resembling the highest spiritual assembly, and comes to stand at the first of the ranks of spiritual beings in perceiving without bodily instruments. So it is always in motion and directed toward that, and it may strip itself entirely from humanity and its spirituality into angelhood, of the highest horizon, without acquisition, but through the constitution and primal innate disposition that God has placed in it for this.
The kinds of human souls

Human souls are of three kinds. One kind is by nature unable to arrive, so its movement stops at the lower direction, toward the sensory and imaginative faculties of perception and the composition of meanings from memory and estimation according to limited rules and a particular order, by which they gain the conceptual and assentive kinds of knowledge that belong to thought in the body. All of it is imaginative, its range confined, since, from the side of its starting point, it ends at the primary truths and does not go beyond them, and if it goes wrong, what comes after them goes wrong. This is for the most part the range of bodily human perception; the perceptions of the scholars end at it, and in it their feet are firmly planted. A second kind is directed by that movement of thought toward the spiritual intellect and a perception that does not need bodily instruments, through the aptitude for it that has been placed in it, so the range of its perception widens beyond the primary truths, which are the range of the first human perception, and it ranges freely in the expanse of inner contemplations, which are all direct experience, with no limit at their beginning or at their end. These are the perceptions of the scholars who are saints, possessors of the religious sciences and divine knowledge, and they are what is attained after death by the people of felicity in the intermediate state (barzakh).
Revelation

And a kind created to strip itself of humanity altogether, its corporeality and its spirituality, to the angels of the highest horizon, so that in a flash it becomes an angel in actuality, and there comes to it the sight of the highest assembly in their horizon and the hearing of the speech of the soul and the divine address in that flash. These are the prophets, God’s blessings and peace be upon them. God made the stripping of humanity in that flash, which is the state of revelation, an innate disposition on which God created them and a constitution in which He formed them, and He kept them clear of the obstacles and impediments of the body, as long as they remain engaged with them through their humanity, by the straightness of purpose and uprightness that He implanted in their instincts, by which they stay in line with that direction; and He fixed in their natures a desire for worship, which is disclosed through that direction and moves readily toward it. So they turn toward that horizon, by that kind of stripping, whenever they wish, through that innate disposition on which they were created, not by acquisition or craft. For that reason they turn and strip themselves of their humanity and receive in that highest assembly what they receive, and they turn with it back to the human faculties of perception, setting it down in their powers, for the wisdom of conveying it to the servants. At one time one of them hears a humming like a veiled hint of speech, from which he takes the meaning that was cast to him, and the humming does not end before he has retained and understood it; and at another time the angel who casts it to him appears to him as a man and speaks with him, and he retains what he says. And the receiving from the angel

and the return to the human faculties of perception and his understanding of what was cast to him — all of it is as if in a single instant, indeed nearer than the blink of an eye, because it is not in time; rather all of it happens together, so it appears as if swift. For that reason it was called revelation (waḥy), since in the language waḥy means haste. Know that the first, which is the state of the humming, is the rank of the prophets who are not messengers, according to what they have verified, and the second, which is the state of the angel appearing as a man who addresses him, is the rank of the prophets who are messengers; for that reason it is more perfect than the first. This is the meaning of the hadith in which the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, explained revelation when al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām asked him and said, “How does revelation come to you?”

He said: “Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and that is the hardest on me; then it leaves me, and I have retained what was said. And sometimes the angel appears to me and speaks to me, and I retain what he says.” The first was harder only because it is the beginning of the passage, in that contact, from potentiality to actuality, so it is somewhat difficult; and for that reason, when he turned in it to the human faculties of perception, it was confined to hearing, and anything else was hard. When revelation is repeated and receiving becomes frequent, that contact becomes easy, so that when he passes back to the human faculties of perception, it reaches all of them, especially the clearest of them, which is the perception of sight. In the expression of retention in the first case in the past tense and in the second in the present tense there is a subtlety of rhetoric: the words came in the manner of a likeness for the two states of revelation. He likened the first state to a humming, which in ordinary usage is not speech, and reported that understanding and retention follow it once it has ended; so it was fitting, in picturing its ending and its breaking off, to express retention in the past tense, which matches ending and cessation. And in the second state he likened the angel to a man who addresses and speaks, and with speech retention goes hand in hand, so it was fitting to express it in the present tense, which implies renewal. Know that in the whole state of revelation there is difficulty overall and hardship, to which the Qurʾān has pointed. The Exalted said:

“We shall cast upon you a weighty word” (73: 5). ʿĀʾisha said: “He used to endure hardship from the sending down,” and she said: “Revelation would come down on him on a very cold day, and then leave him, and his forehead would be streaming with sweat.” For that reason there would arise in him in that state the absence and the snoring that are well known. The reason for that is that revelation, as we have established, is a departure from humanity to the angelic faculties of perception and a receiving of the speech of the soul, so a hardship arises from it from the self’s separation from itself and its stripping away from itself, from its own horizon to that other horizon. This is the meaning of the squeezing mentioned at the beginning of revelation in his words: “He squeezed me until the strain had reached its utmost in me, then released me, and he said, ‘Read.’ I said, ‘I am not a reader.’ And so a second time and a third,” as in the hadith. Habit may gradually, little by little, lead to some ease compared with what went before; and for that reason the portions of the Qurʾān that came down, its suras and its verses, when he was in Mecca were shorter than when he was in Medina. Consider what is reported about the revelation of the sura Barāʾa on the expedition to Tabūk, that all of it, or most of it, came down on him as he rode on his she-camel, whereas in Mecca part of a sura of the short suras of the Mufaṣṣal would come down at one time and the rest at another. Likewise the last thing to come down in Medina was the verse of debt, and what a length it has, whereas in Mecca verses used to come down like the verses of al-Raḥmān, al-Dhāriyāt, al-Muddaththir, al-Ḍuḥā, al-Falaq and the like. Take from this a sign by which to tell the Meccan from the Medinan among suras and verses; and God is the guide to what is right. This is the sum of the matter of prophecy.
Soothsaying

As for soothsaying, it too is among the properties of the human soul. For it was shown earlier, in everything that has gone before, that the human soul has an aptitude for stripping itself of humanity into the spirituality that is above it, that a flash of this occurs for human beings in the class of the prophets through the innate disposition on which they were created for it, and that it was established that it occurs for them without acquisition and without recourse to any of the faculties of perception, or of conceptions, or of bodily acts, whether speech or movement, or to any other thing; it is only a stripping of humanity into angelhood by innate disposition, in a moment nearer than the blink of an eye. If that is so, and that aptitude exists in human nature, then the rational division yields that there is here another class of human beings, falling short of the rank of the first class as an opposite falls short of its perfect opposite, because the absence of recourse to aids in that perception is the opposite of recourse to aids in it, and how far apart they are. When the division of existence yields here another class of human beings, innately disposed so that its rational power moves in its movement of thought by volition whenever longing for that stirs it, but is by constitution deficient in it, then when incapacity keeps it from this, it clings to particular matters, sensed or imagined, such as translucent bodies, the bones of animals, rhymed prose (sajʿ), and any bird or animal that happens to cross its path

so it keeps up that sensing or imagining, drawing on it as an aid in the stripping that it intends, and it becomes like an escort to it. This power in them, which is the origin of that perception, is soothsaying. Because these souls are innately disposed to deficiency and shortfall from perfection, their perception is more in particulars than in universals. For that reason the imaginative faculty in them is extremely strong, because it is the instrument of particulars, so it penetrates them fully, in sleep or waking, and they are present and ready before the soul, brought forward by the imaginative faculty, which is for the soul like a mirror in which it constantly looks. The soothsayer is not strong enough to reach perfection in the perception of intelligibles, because his inspiration is of the inspiration of the devil. The highest state of this class is to resort to speech containing rhymed prose and balance, in order to be occupied with it away from the senses and to be somewhat strengthened for that incomplete contact, so that from that movement, and from the extraneous thing that accompanies it, something comes into his heart, which he casts onto his tongue. At times it is true and agrees with the truth, and at times it is false, because he completes his deficiency by something extraneous to his perceiving essence, distinct from it and unsuited to it, so both truth and falsehood befall him, and he is not to be trusted. At times he resorts to conjectures and guesses, out of eagerness to succeed in the perception, by his own claim, and to mislead those who ask. The practitioners of this rhymed prose are the ones specially called soothsayers, because they are the highest of all their kinds

And the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said of the like of it: “This is of the rhymed prose of the soothsayers,” making rhymed prose specific to them by the force of the genitive construction. And he said to Ibn Ṣayyād, when he questioned him to uncover his condition by his reports, “How does this matter come to you?” He said: “It comes to me truthful and false.” He said: “The matter has been confused for you.” He meant that the characteristic of prophecy is truth, so falsehood never touches it, because it is a connection of the prophet’s essence with the highest assembly without an escort and without recourse to anything extraneous. As for soothsaying, since its practitioner, because of his incapacity, needed to resort to extraneous conceptions, these entered into his perception and became confused with the perception to which he was turning, so that it became mixed with them, and falsehood found its way to him from this direction; so it is impossible for it to be prophecy. We said that the highest of the ranks of soothsaying is the state of rhymed prose only because the meaning of rhymed prose is lighter than the other hidden things, of things seen and heard; and the lightness of the meaning indicates the nearness of that contact and perception, and some distance in it from incapacity.

And some people have claimed that this soothsaying has ceased since the time of prophecy, because of the stoning of the devils with shooting stars that took place just before the mission, and that this was to bar them from news of heaven, as is stated in the Qurʾān, and the soothsayers learn the news of heaven only from the devils, so soothsaying became void from that day. But no proof stands from that, because the knowledge of the soothsayers, just as it comes from the devils, also comes from their own souls, as we have established. Also, the verse indicates only the barring of the devils from one kind of news of heaven, namely what relates to the news of the mission; they were not barred from anything other than that. Also, that cessation was only just before prophecy, and perhaps it returned afterward to what it had been; and this is the likelier view, because all these faculties of perception are dimmed in the time of prophecy, as the stars and lamps are dimmed when the sun is present, for prophecy is the greatest light, in whose presence every other light is hidden and goes away.
